meta.topics: China, EU, industrial policy, currency, autos

L0.text: Why is Europe losing ground to China in trade, and what should it do about it?

L1.text: China's trade war tools are industrial policy and a weak currency, not tariffs
Chinese firms, private or state-linked, accept low returns on equity and build too much
A trading partner's surplus drains demand from your economy; manufacturing capacity has strategic value beyond its profits

L2.text: European exports to China down about 0.5 percentage points of European GDP; EU trade deficit with China set to double between 2020 and 2025; European auto exports to China on track for about $10 billion by 2027; Chinese electric vehicle exports at a 3 million annual pace in the second quarter; net exports added about 2 percentage points to Chinese growth over four quarters; yuan weaker against the euro
Centre for European Reform brief on German industry; Financial Times, New York Times and Wall Street Journal sector reporting; Adam Tooze; German customs data

L3.text: Competing local governments add subsidized capacity, which drives profits down and pushes output China cannot absorb into exports
State banks keep the yuan weak; its fall against the euro has roughly offset the EU's 17 percent countervailing duty on BYD

L4.header: Intermediate claim
L4.text: The second China shock is eroding Europe's core export sectors and is large enough to matter for the whole economy, especially Germany's stagnation

L5.text: China is winning a trade war with Europe; Europe needs a counter-industrial policy, broader tariffs on Chinese autos and new pressure for the yuan to rise

L6.text: Europe's inadequate response so far; Trump-style tariffs or commodity purchase deals as the fix
The United States is still importing, which limits the damage, but American firms will not absorb tariff costs much longer
China's long-standing tariff walls (25 percent on autos) also helped build the sector

meta.title: The Trump Shock That Wasn't (At Least Not Yet)
meta.author: Brad W. Setser
meta.topics: US tariffs, trade flows, elasticities, WTO

L0.text: Have Trump's tariffs actually shocked trade flows and the global economy?

L1.text: A global tariff works like an exchange rate move: import elasticity of about 0.3 to 0.4, not the bilateral elasticity of about 2
Record tariff revenue means Americans keep importing and paying the tariff
Tax- and finance-driven flows (pharmaceuticals, gold) are noise; core trade is the real signal

L2.text: Annualized trade deficit peaked at $2 trillion in March, fell to $1 trillion, then rebounded to $1.2 trillion in July; imports from Taiwan up over 50 percent year to date; first-term tariffs cut affected trade about 30 percent, and about 50 percent for goods tariffed at 25 percent; high-frequency global trade measures have not slowed
New York Times reporting; U.S. trade data; federal court ruling on tariff authority

L3.text: Pharmaceutical stockpiling (distorted by tax) and gold flows drive the headline swings
Imports shift from China to Taiwan and Southeast Asia as final assembly relocates
The data center buildout pushes electronics imports up
A 15 percent tariff times a 0.3 to 0.4 elasticity cuts imports 5 to 6 percent; non-oil imports fall from about 10 to 9.5 percent of GDP

L4.header: Intermediate claim
L4.text: Excluding pharmaceuticals and gold, U.S. imports are roughly on trend; the shock to trade rules far exceeds the shock to trade flows

L5.text: The Trump shock to trade flows has not happened yet, though a modest impact should appear

L6.text: Reading headline volatility as tariffs crushing trade
August deals doubled tariffs on Southeast Asia relative to April; fall data may show more impact; the tariffs' legality is unresolved
Waiting for tariff relief (autos) replaces front-running; other exporters can take U.S. market share abroad

meta.title: China's Massive Surplus is Everywhere (Yet The IMF Still Has Trouble Seeing It Clearly)
meta.author: Brad W. Setser
meta.topics: China, IMF, global imbalances, fiscal policy

L0.text: How big is China's surplus really, why does the IMF miss it, and what policy should follow?

L1.text: The surplus stems from a shortfall in China's domestic demand (European Central Bank view)
Deflation combined with a rising trade surplus calls for sustained fiscal expansion, not monetary easing
External balance is a legitimate policy target; exporting your way out of a slump imposes costs on other countries

L2.text: Export volumes up 40 percent since end-2019 versus imports up 1 percent; manufactured goods surplus over $2 trillion (about 10.5 percent of GDP); goods surplus $1.2 trillion; car exports over 6 million, heading toward 8 million in 2026; current account surplus 2.2 percent of GDP versus the EU's 2.6 percent; IMF forecast a 2025 surplus of $375 billion, while the actual tops $650 billion through the third quarter

IMF External Sector Report 2025, October World Economic Outlook and 2024 Article IV report; European Central Bank analysis; Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis export volume data; Microsoft annual report

L3.text: Weak domestic demand leaves spare capacity for exports; rate cuts lower yields and weaken the yuan, widening the surplus
The 2022 balance of payments methodology and the unexplained income deficit each cut about 1 percentage point of GDP from the reported current account surplus
Relying only on the reported current account frames China's problem as purely internal, so the IMF prescribes monetary easing

L4.header: Intermediate claim
L4.text: China's surplus is massive and growing, yet IMF policy advice effectively lets China export its way out of its housing slump

L5.text: The IMF should recognize China's external imbalance and call for a fiscal expansion funded by the central government

L6.text: The IMF's framing; the argument that Europe's surplus is almost as big
China's GDP data are too thin to confirm the net export math; the IMF does support pro-consumption structural reforms
Ireland distorts European data; IMF forecast misses come from ignoring lagged exchange rate effects and treating the pandemic surge as temporary

meta.title: Understanding the Low October 2025 Trade Deficit
meta.author: Brad W. Setser
meta.topics: US trade deficit, tariffs, stockpiling, fiscal policy

L0.text: Does the low October 2025 trade deficit mean the tariffs are working?

L1.text: Tariffs reduce the trade deficit only if their proceeds reduce the budget deficit, acting as a tax hike
Remove pharmaceuticals and gold to read the underlying deficit
The trade balance is a macroeconomic savings-investment outcome; inventory swings reverse over time

L2.text: October's drop came entirely from pharmaceuticals and gold; excluding them, October's deficit was slightly bigger than September's; August to October deficits below 2024, but early 2025 far above; imports of autos and household durable goods down; imports of semiconductors and computers up
U.S. trade data; Section 232 semiconductor investigation

L3.text: Fear of tariffs that never came drove pharmaceutical stockpiling and gold flowing out and back
Stockpiles built ahead of tariffs temporarily depress imports, and stockpiles run out
The data center buildout keeps semiconductor and computer imports rising
Promised refund checks and pressure for more defense spending block a fiscal adjustment

L4.header: Intermediate claim
L4.text: Tariffs reduce imports in specific categories, but the overall deficit is driven by untariffed goods and stockpile timing

L5.text: No: the low October deficit is not evidence the tariffs work, and a significant fall in the 2025 deficit is unlikely

L6.text: Trump's trade team claiming success from smaller deficits than in the same months of 2024
Tariffed categories really are falling; watch whether imports rebound once stockpiles are exhausted
Auto imports fell along with auto sales: weaker demand rather than more U.S. production
